clinician.trajectory_summary: An 80-year-old man with hypertension, glaucoma, and first-degree heart block presented with a 3-month history of frontal headaches. Initial CT head was unremarkable for intracranial pathology but incidentally revealed a left ventral thalamus lacunar infarct. Three days after CT imaging, during a routine ophthalmology glaucoma follow-up appointment, the ophthalmologist elicited a history of diplopia, amaurosis fugax, and significant weight loss over the preceding months. Physical examination revealed bilateral tender, nodular, and weakly pulsatile temporal arteries. Temporal and axillary artery ultrasound demonstrated a characteristic halo sign in the right temporal artery. Despite only mildly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 11 mg/L, ESR 15 mm/hour), clinical suspicion for GCA was high due to vision-threatening symptoms and jaw claudication. Right temporal artery biopsy was performed and revealed a muscular artery with focal adventitial chronic inflammation and intimal hyperplasia with mild inflammation, confirming GCA. High-dose prednisolone (60 mg) was initiated immediately per British Society of Rheumatology guidelines. At 4-week follow-up, symptoms improved significantly and inflammatory markers normalized (CRP <3, ESR 2).
